title: Does a Straw Get You Drunk Faster? The Science of the Straw Myth
excerpt: Does drinking through a straw get you drunk faster? Why the vacuum and vapor myths don't hold up, what really speeds up alcohol absorption, and how pace changes everything.
metaDescription: Does drinking through a straw get you drunk faster? Why the vacuum myth is wrong, what really speeds alcohol absorption, and why pace matters most.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no, a straw does not change how your body absorbs alcohol. The same drink, consumed over the same amount of time, produces the same blood alcohol level whether it goes through a straw, a glass, or a bottle. The popular explanations (that a straw creates a vacuum that "vaporizes" alcohol, that it sends alcohol straight to your brain, or that it lets alcohol soak in under your tongue) don't hold up. What a straw *can* change is your pace. If it makes you finish a drink faster, you'll get drunk faster, the same way you would if you gulped from the glass. It's about pace, not vapor.

**The quick version:** How drunk you get depends on how much alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, whether you've eaten, your body size and sex, and a few details like carbonation and mixer type. The drinking vessel isn't on that list. If you notice you get tipsy faster with straws, look at what you're drinking through them (usually sweet, cold, easy-to-drink cocktails) and how quickly the glass empties.

> **Safety note.** This article explains how alcohol absorption works. It is not medical advice. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't let them "sleep it off," and don't leave them alone. In the US, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) can also advise.

## Does Drinking Through a Straw Get You Drunk Faster?

Not directly. The straw myth usually comes in one of a few forms:

- "Sucking through a straw creates a vacuum, and the low pressure turns alcohol into vapor that hits you harder."
- "A straw bypasses your taste buds and shoots alcohol straight to the back of your throat, so it absorbs faster."
- "Alcohol gets absorbed through the inside of your mouth, and a straw concentrates it there."
- "You swallow more air with a straw, and the air speeds up absorption."

None of these change where or how fast alcohol enters your blood in any meaningful way. To see why, it helps to know where absorption actually happens.

## Where Alcohol Actually Gets Absorbed

Alcohol (ethanol) is a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat, so it crosses the lining of your digestive tract easily. But not all parts of the tract are equal:

- **Mouth and throat:** a trivial amount. Drinks pass through in a second or two, and the surface area is tiny.
- **Stomach:** some absorption, roughly a fifth of the total by most textbook estimates. The stomach also breaks down a small share of the alcohol before it ever reaches your blood, using an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase. This "first-pass" effect is larger when there's food in the stomach.
- **Small intestine:** the main event. The upper small intestine has an enormous surface area and absorbs alcohol very quickly. Most of the alcohol in any drink enters your bloodstream here.

That last point is the key to the whole question. Because the small intestine does most of the absorbing, **the biggest single factor in how fast alcohol hits your blood is how quickly your stomach empties into your small intestine.** This is called gastric emptying. Anything that keeps alcohol in the stomach longer (mainly food) slows absorption and lowers your peak blood alcohol. Anything that rushes it through (an empty stomach, drinking a lot in a short time) speeds absorption and raises the peak.

A straw doesn't touch any of this. Once the liquid is in your mouth, your body has no way of knowing how it got there. Your stomach and small intestine handle it exactly the same.

For a deeper look at how food changes this, see our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

## The "Vacuum Vaporizes Alcohol" Myth

This is the most common version of the claim, and it sounds scientific, so it's worth taking apart.

The idea goes like this: sucking on a straw lowers the pressure inside it, lower pressure lowers the boiling point of liquids, so some alcohol turns into vapor, and alcohol vapor gets absorbed through your lungs much faster than liquid through your gut.

There are a few problems with that chain:

1. **The pressure drop is tiny.** When you sip through a straw, you lower the pressure in your mouth by only a small fraction of normal air pressure, just enough to lift liquid a few inches. To make ethanol boil at room temperature, you'd need to drop the pressure dramatically, far beyond what human lungs and cheeks can do.
2. **The liquid isn't pure alcohol.** Even a strong cocktail is mostly water, mixer, and ice. Ethanol in a diluted, cold drink is even less inclined to evaporate.
3. **You're not inhaling the drink.** When you sip through a straw, you create suction with your mouth and the liquid travels to your tongue. You aren't drawing that air down into your lungs. Any trace of vapor at the surface of the drink is the same trace you'd smell from an open glass.

The reason this myth persists is that inhaling alcohol vapor *is* a real (and dangerous) thing. Devices that nebulize or vaporize alcohol for inhalation exist, and health authorities warn against them because alcohol absorbed through the lungs skips the stomach's first-pass breakdown and can't be vomited back up if you've had too much. But that requires a device built to aerosolize alcohol. A drinking straw doesn't come close.

## The "Absorbed Under Your Tongue" Myth

Some medicines are designed to dissolve under the tongue (sublingual) because the tissue there absorbs certain drugs quickly. People sometimes assume alcohol works the same way, and that a straw somehow delivers it to that spot.

In practice, the amount of alcohol absorbed in your mouth while drinking is negligible. Sublingual medicines work because they're held in place for minutes. A sip of a drink is in your mouth for a second or two before you swallow. And a straw usually delivers liquid toward the middle or back of your tongue, not underneath it. Either way, the drink ends up in the same place: your stomach.

## The "Straws Make You Swallow Air" Theory

This one has a kernel of truth. Drinking through a straw can make you swallow a little more air, and that's why some people say straws make them feel bloated or gassy.

Could swallowed air speed absorption? There's no good evidence that it does in any way that matters. The more interesting related question is carbonation, because carbon dioxide in a drink is a lot more gas than the air you'd swallow through a straw, and carbonation *has* been studied. We cover that below.

## So Why Do People Feel Drunker With a Straw?

If you've ever felt that cocktails through a straw hit harder, you're probably not imagining the result. You're just pinning it on the wrong cause. Here's what's more likely going on.

### 1. You drink faster without noticing

This is the big one. With a glass, you see and feel each sip: you tilt it, you taste it, you set it down. With a straw, especially a wide one in a tall glass full of ice, it's easy to take long, continuous pulls while you're talking or dancing. You don't see the level dropping until you hit the bottom and hear that slurping sound.

Drinking speed matters a lot. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, and you can't speed that up. If you drink two cocktails in 30 minutes instead of over two hours, more alcohol hits your bloodstream at once and your peak blood alcohol concentration (BAC, the share of alcohol in your blood) climbs higher. You'll feel it more, and sooner.

### 2. Straw drinks tend to be the strongest, easiest-to-drink ones

Think about which drinks come with straws: frozen margaritas, daiquiris, piña coladas, Long Island iced teas, mai tais, "fishbowls," and big sugary punches. These tend to:

- **Contain more than one standard drink.** A Long Island iced tea commonly contains four or five spirits. A large frozen margarita may hold two or more shots. Fishbowls are often meant to be shared but get treated like a single drink.
- **Hide the taste of alcohol.** Sugar, fruit juice, and cold temperature all mask the burn of alcohol, so you don't get the natural "slow down" signal you'd get from sipping straight spirits.
- **Go down fast.** Cold, sweet, slushy drinks are refreshing, and people finish them quickly, especially in the heat.

So "drinks I have through a straw" often means "stronger drinks I drink faster." That's a real reason to feel drunker, and it has nothing to do with the straw itself.

### 3. Smaller sips are harder to count

Some people argue the opposite: that a straw slows them down because each sip is small. That can be true too. The point is that the straw changes your *habits*, and habits vary from person to person. Whichever way the straw nudges your pace is the way it nudges your BAC.

### 4. Expectation plays a part

How drunk you *feel* isn't only about your BAC. Research on alcohol expectancy (studies where people are given placebo drinks they believe contain alcohol) has shown that what people expect a drink to do can shape how impaired they feel and act. If you've heard straws get you drunk faster, you may notice and attribute your buzz to the straw. That doesn't change your actual blood alcohol, but it can change your experience of it.

## The Things That Actually Change How Fast You Get Drunk

If you want to understand (or control) how quickly alcohol hits you, these are the factors that matter. A straw isn't one of them.

### How much alcohol you drink

The total amount of pure alcohol is the starting point. In the US, one "standard drink" contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly a 12-ounce beer at 5% alcohol, a 5-ounce glass of wine at 12%, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 40% spirits. Many cocktails and craft beers contain well over one standard drink. Our guide on [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) breaks this down by body weight and drink type.

### How fast you drink it

Covered above. Pace is the factor a straw can actually affect, and it's one of the most important things you control on a night out.

### Whether you've eaten

Food is the single best brake on absorption. A meal, especially one with protein, fat, and fiber, keeps alcohol in your stomach longer, gives the stomach's enzymes more time to break some of it down, and spreads the rest out so it reaches your small intestine more slowly. Studies comparing drinking on a full versus an empty stomach consistently show lower and later peak BAC with food. Drinking on an empty stomach does the reverse.

### Your body size and sex

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A larger person generally has more body water, so the same drink produces a lower concentration. On average, women have a lower share of body water than men of the same weight, and some research suggests less first-pass breakdown in the stomach, so the same drink tends to produce a higher BAC in women. Our explainer on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) goes into the details.

### Carbonation

This is where the "gas" part of the straw myth gets interesting. Some research suggests carbonated drinks can raise blood alcohol faster than flat ones. A small UK study published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* (Ridout and colleagues, 2003) found that people drinking fizzy champagne reached higher blood alcohol levels sooner than when they drank the same champagne gone flat. Another small study (Roberts and Robinson, 2007, *Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine*) found that mixing vodka with a carbonated mixer led to faster absorption for most participants than mixing it with still water, though not for everyone.

The likely explanation is that the gas speeds up stomach emptying, pushing alcohol into the small intestine sooner. These studies were small and results varied between people, so treat this as "carbonation may speed things up a bit," not a hard rule. It's also unrelated to straws, since the gas comes from the drink.

### Alcohol concentration

Moderately concentrated drinks, in roughly the 20% to 30% range, tend to be absorbed fastest. Very dilute drinks like light beer are absorbed more slowly because there's simply more liquid to get through. Very strong drinks like straight spirits can irritate the stomach lining and slow stomach emptying somewhat, though people who take several shots quickly still get a big dose fast.

### Diet versus regular mixers

A study by Marczinski and Stamates (*Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, 2013) found that people who drank vodka mixed with a diet soft drink had higher breath alcohol levels than when they drank the same amount of vodka with a regular sugary soft drink. The sugar in a regular mixer seems to slow stomach emptying a little, while artificial sweeteners don't. Again, it's the contents of the glass that matter, not the straw in it.

### Medications and health conditions

Some medicines, as well as conditions that change how fast your stomach empties, can affect how quickly alcohol hits you or how strongly you feel it. If you take any regular medication, it's worth asking a pharmacist whether it interacts with alcohol.

## A Quick Myth-Check Table

| Claim | Verdict | What's actually going on |
|---|---|---|
| A straw creates a vacuum that vaporizes alcohol | False | The suction from a straw is far too weak to make alcohol boil, and you aren't inhaling the drink |
| Alcohol through a straw absorbs in your mouth | False | Mouth absorption is negligible; most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine |
| You get drunk faster with a straw | Sometimes, indirectly | Only if the straw makes you drink faster, or the straw drink is stronger |
| Swallowing air through a straw speeds absorption | No good evidence | It may cause bloating, but it isn't known to raise BAC meaningfully |
| Fizzy drinks hit faster | Possibly | Small studies suggest carbonation may speed absorption for some people |
| Diet mixers hit faster than sugary ones | Some evidence | One controlled study found higher breath alcohol with diet mixers |
| Eating first slows absorption | True | Food delays stomach emptying and lowers peak BAC |

## Does a Straw Make Any Difference to Your Hangover?

Not on its own. Hangovers are driven mainly by how much you drink, along with dehydration, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, inflammation, and by-products of alcohol breakdown such as acetaldehyde. Some drinks may make hangovers worse for some people (darker spirits contain more congeners, which are other compounds produced during fermentation), but the straw is irrelevant.

The indirect effect is the same as before: if straws lead you to drink more, or faster, you'll likely feel worse the next day. Sugary frozen cocktails can also make it easy to lose count, which is a common route to a rough morning.

If you want to cut your hangover risk, the practical steps are well known: eat before and while drinking, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, choose drinks you can count, and stop at a number you've decided ahead of time. Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the evidence for each.

## Practical Tips If You Want to Drink Slower

Since pace is the part of this you actually control, here are some simple ways to keep it in check, straw or no straw:

1. **Eat a real meal first.** It's the most effective way to slow absorption and blunt your peak BAC.
2. **Know what's in the glass.** Ask the bartender how many shots go into a cocktail, or check the menu. Treat a Long Island iced tea or a large frozen drink as more than one drink.
3. **Set a per-hour pace.** Roughly one standard drink an hour roughly matches what your liver can clear. You'll still feel effects, but you won't stack them up as quickly.
4. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and helps with hydration.
5. **Put the drink down.** If you're holding a drink with a straw, it's easy to sip on autopilot. Setting it down between sips breaks the habit.
6. **Skip the shared fishbowl, or count your share honestly.** Group drinks make it almost impossible to track what you've had.
7. **Be careful with diet mixers and fizzy drinks if you're trying to go slow**, since the evidence suggests they may get alcohol into your blood a bit faster.

For more strategies, see our guide on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk) when you're drinking socially.

## How Long Until a Drink Hits You?

For most people, alcohol starts to show up in the blood within minutes of drinking, and blood alcohol typically peaks somewhere around 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, depending largely on whether you've eaten. On an empty stomach the peak comes sooner and higher; after a meal it comes later and lower.

This lag is why people often feel "fine" and order another round, only to feel the full effect half an hour later. It's also why a straw drink you finished quickly can seem to "suddenly" hit you. The alcohol was always on its way. You just drank it faster than your brain could register.

Once alcohol is in your blood, only time clears it. Coffee, cold showers, and food after the fact don't speed up your liver. Our guide on [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) explains the timeline.

## Where Supplements Fit In

No supplement makes it safe to drink faster or more, and nothing changes the basic math of alcohol, pace, and food. That said, some people who drink socially use a supplement as one small part of their routine. The one we cover most is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Animal research and lab studies suggest it may support the body's processing of alcohol and its by-products, but human data is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents intoxication, lowers your blood alcohol, or prevents hangovers in everyone.

If you want to try it, look for a product with a clearly labeled DHM dose. A straightforward single-ingredient option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). A combination formula some people prefer is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

Treat any supplement as a minor add-on. Eating, pacing, and water still do the heavy lifting.

## The Bottom Line

- A straw doesn't change how your body absorbs alcohol. Most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine, and the vessel you drink from has no effect on that.
- The "vacuum vaporizes the alcohol" idea doesn't work. The suction from a straw is far too weak, and you aren't inhaling the drink.
- Straws can get you drunk faster indirectly, by making it easy to drink quickly and by coming with strong, sweet cocktails that hide the alcohol.
- The real factors are how much you drink, how fast, whether you've eaten, your body size and sex, and to a smaller degree carbonation and diet mixers.
- If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning (confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or pale or bluish skin), call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does drinking through a straw get you drunk faster?**

Not directly. Your body absorbs alcohol the same way no matter how it reaches your mouth, mostly through the small intestine. A straw can get you drunk faster indirectly if it makes you drink more quickly, or if the drinks served with straws are stronger and sweeter. The amount you drink and your pace matter, not the straw.

**Does a straw create a vacuum that vaporizes alcohol?**

No. Sipping through a straw lowers the pressure in your mouth only slightly, far too little to make alcohol boil or evaporate in any meaningful amount. You also aren't inhaling the drink, so any trace of vapor never reaches your lungs. Inhaling alcohol vapor is a real hazard, but it takes a device designed to aerosolize alcohol, not a drinking straw.

**Is alcohol absorbed in your mouth when you use a straw?**

Only a negligible amount. A sip stays in your mouth for a second or two before you swallow. About a fifth of alcohol is absorbed in the stomach and most of the rest in the small intestine, which is why food and stomach emptying matter far more than how the drink enters your mouth.

**Why do I feel drunker when I drink with a straw?**

Most likely because you're drinking faster without noticing, or because straw drinks such as frozen margaritas, Long Island iced teas, and fishbowls often hold more than one standard drink and hide the taste of alcohol. Expectation can also play a part: if you believe straws make you drunker, you may notice your buzz more.

**Do fizzy drinks get you drunk faster?**

Possibly. Small studies have found that carbonated drinks, such as fizzy champagne or vodka with a carbonated mixer, raised blood alcohol faster than flat versions for many participants, likely because the gas speeds stomach emptying. Results varied between people. One study also found diet mixers led to higher breath alcohol than sugary ones.

**What actually makes you get drunk faster?**

Drinking more alcohol in less time, drinking on an empty stomach, being smaller, and, on average, being female all raise blood alcohol faster. Carbonated drinks and diet mixers may speed absorption a little. Eating a meal first is the most effective way to slow it down.

**Does drinking through a straw make your hangover worse?**

Not on its own. Hangovers depend mainly on how much you drink, along with dehydration, poor sleep, and the by-products of alcohol breakdown. A straw only matters if it leads you to drink more or faster than you otherwise would.

**Can DHM stop you from getting drunk?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents intoxication or lowers blood alcohol in people. Some animal and lab research suggests it may support how the body processes alcohol, but human data is limited. It doesn't make it safe to drink faster or more.
